message.content:
The 19th‑century sculpture world was rich with masterpieces, but if you’re looking for the single work that most people think of when they hear “famous 19th‑century sculpture,” it’s almost always **“The Kiss” (Le Baiser) by Auguste Rodin** (1889).

### Why “The Kiss” stands out

| Feature | Details |
|---------|---------|
| **Artist** | Auguste Rodin, a leading French sculptor who helped usher in modern sculpture |
| **Date** | 1889 (first cast) |
| **Material** | Bronze (originally a plaster model) |
| **Style** | Realist/Impressionist, capturing intimate human emotion |
| **Impact** | Became an icon of romantic love; widely reproduced, displayed in museums worldwide, and referenced in countless works of art and popular culture |
| **Legacy** | Often cited as a turning point in sculpture, moving away from idealized forms toward more naturalistic, emotionally charged subjects |

### Other contenders

While “The Kiss” is the most instantly recognizable, several other 19th‑century sculptures also command a place in the canon:

| Sculpture | Artist | Year | Significance |
|-----------|--------|------|--------------|
| **The Gates of Hell** | Rodin | 1880–1917 (unfinished) | A monumental, complex work that influenced modern sculpture and architecture |
| **The Statue of Liberty** | Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi | 1886 | A monumental public sculpture symbolizing freedom, now a global icon |
| **The Thinker** | Rodin | 1902 (late 19th‑early 20th) | Though technically early 20th, it’s often grouped with late 19th‑century works and remains iconic |
| **The Venus de Milo** (recast) | Various | 2000s (based on 2nd‑century original) | Not a 19th‑century creation, but its 19th‑century restorations and popularity made it a cultural touchstone |

### Bottom line

If you’re asked to name the most famous sculpture of the 19th century, “The Kiss” by Rodin is the answer most people will give. It captures the era’s shift toward realism, emotional depth, and the celebration of everyday human experience—an ethos that defined much of 19th‑century art.
